title: Social Studies: Votes, Taxes, and Trade
objectives: I can use ten words about government, voting, and money to describe how a town works.
I can explain how supply and demand can change the price of a product.
I can tell what a mayor, a candidate, and a lawmaker each do.
I can write about a community decision using words from this unit.
rationale: Fifth-grade social studies introduces how communities make decisions and how money moves through them. Economy, supply, and demand are the three core economic terms students meet, and tax and burden connect economics to government. Elect, candidate, ballot, mayor, and lawmaker are the core civics words that students need to read about elections and to take part in a classroom vote. The passage describes an invented town so that all ten words appear together in one coherent system. The unit revisits proof, debate, injustice, and viewpoint from the argument and fairness units, because citizens use those ideas whenever they weigh candidates or debate a tax.

words.def: The system by which a place makes, buys, and sells goods and services.

words.def: Something heavy or hard to carry, such as a cost or a duty.

passage.title: How Riverton Decides
paras: The town of Riverton has a small economy built on farms, a bakery, and a busy hardware store. Like every economy, it depends on supply and demand. When a hard frost ruined most of the apple crop, the supply of apples dropped. Many families still wanted apples for pies, so demand stayed high, and the price at the market climbed.

The town also depends on taxes. Each household pays a small tax, and the money pays for roads, the library, and the fire department. Some residents feel the tax is a burden, especially when prices rise. Others say it is a fair price for services that everyone uses.

This fall, Riverton will elect a new mayor. Two candidates, Ms. Reyes and Mr. Kim, have visited every neighborhood to explain their ideas. Ms. Reyes wants to repair the old bridge, and Mr. Kim wants to add a bus line. On Election Day, registered voters will mark a ballot in private, and the votes will be counted that night.

After the election, the new mayor will work with the town's lawmakers, who meet each month to vote on new rules. A mayor cannot pass a law alone. Citizens who pay attention to the economy, the taxes, and the candidates help the whole town decide wisely.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "supply" refers to
choices: the number of buyers in a store
the amount of apples that was available
the price on a sign
the cost of fixing a farm
qs.why: The frost ruined most of the apple crop, so the supply, meaning the amount available, dropped.

qs.q: Why did the price of apples climb at the market?
choices: The supply fell while demand stayed high.
The bakery stopped buying apples.
The town lowered its taxes.
Fewer families wanted pie.
qs.why: The text says supply dropped but many families still wanted apples, so demand stayed high and the price climbed.

qs.q: Which detail best shows what taxes in Riverton pay for?
choices: The mayor will work with lawmakers.
Roads, the library, and the fire department.
The apple crop at the market.
A new bus line.
qs.why: The paragraph says the tax money pays for roads, the library, and the fire department.

qs.q: What does the author mean by saying some residents think the tax is a burden?
choices: They feel it is hard to carry, especially when prices rise.
They believe it should be higher.
They do not know what it pays for.
They think the mayor invented it.
qs.why: A burden is something heavy to bear, and the text links the feeling to rising prices.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Apples are the most important crop in town.
Mayors can pass any law they wish.
Voters should never pay taxes.
A town's economy, taxes, and elections all connect, and citizens help decide how they work.
qs.why: Each paragraph covers one part of how Riverton works, and the last says citizens who pay attention help the town decide wisely.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for how a community runs: three economic terms (economy, supply, demand), two money-and-government terms (tax, burden), and five civics words (elect, candidate, ballot, mayor, lawmaker). The passage describes an invented town so students can see the ideas connect. Writing and discussion ask students to take a viewpoint on a tax or a vote and support it.

notes.va.economy.n: Economy is the system by which a place makes, buys, and sells goods and services. Students may think it means money only. Show a simple diagram with farms, stores, workers, and buyers in a loop.
notes.va.supply.n: Supply is how much is available. Students often confuse it with supplies, classroom materials. Connect to a store shelf that is full or empty. Pair with demand on a see-saw sketch.
notes.va.demand.n: Demand is how much people want to buy, and the economics sense is different from the everyday verb to demand. Use the apple example. Note that prices usually rise when demand is high and supply is low, but many things can change a price.
notes.va.tax.n: A tax is money paid to the government for public services. Students may think a tax is a fee or a fine. Contrast: a fine is a penalty, a tax pays for roads and schools. Have students list what taxes pay for.
notes.va.elect.v: To elect is to choose by voting. Students may confuse elect with select. Elect is for offices, and the noun is election. Run a class vote and have students use the word in a sentence.
notes.va.candidate.n: A candidate is a person running for office, and the word can also mean a person who applies for a job. Tie the word to the passage. Ask what a candidate should explain to voters.
notes.va.ballot.n: A ballot is the paper, or screen, used to vote. Students may think it means the whole election. Mention secret ballot: no one sees how you voted. Make a classroom ballot and use it.
notes.va.lawmaker.n: A lawmaker makes laws. In the town of Riverton the lawmakers are council members. Students may think the mayor makes all laws; clarify that mayors and lawmakers share different jobs.
notes.va.burden.n: Burden has a literal sense, a heavy load a person carries, and an extended sense, a cost or duty hard to bear. Teach both, since the passage uses the extended one. Ask students to act out carrying a burden and to name a burden in their lives, such as homework.
notes.va.mayor.n: A mayor is the elected leader of a city or town. Students may confuse mayor with major. Say the words aloud: MAY-er and MAY-jer. Ask what jobs a mayor does in your area.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The text says a frost ruined most of the apple crop, so there were fewer apples available. That is the supply. Families still wanted apples for pies, so demand stayed high. When there are few apples and many buyers, the price tends to climb. Each detail fits one of the new words.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit proof, debate, injustice, and viewpoint by asking students to debate whether a tax is fair, to name the proof they would need, and to decide whether any group might see it as an injustice. Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, using news headlines about local government.

needsReview: Riverton, Ms. Reyes, Mr. Kim, and the apple frost are invented; the economic and civic statements (supply and demand affecting price, taxes paying for public services, secret ballots, mayors and councils) are standard but simplified and not checked against a cited source.

Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: oferta (supply), demanda (demand; cognate in economics only), impuesto (tax), boleta electoral (ballot; papeleta in Spain), legislador (lawmaker), alcalde (mayor), carga (burden).
The teacher note for mayor gives MAY-er and MAY-jer as pronunciations; standard but not checked against a dictionary.
